title: Accelerating ab initio melting property calculations with machine learning: application to the high entropy alloy TaVCrW

recollection.starting_material: The high‐entropy alloy (HEA) Ta–V–Cr–W, which adopts a single BCC solid solution at ambient conditions
recollection.intervention: Development of a machine-learning interatomic potential (e.g., moment tensor or SNAP) trained on a small but judiciously chosen set of DFT data, followed by large-scale molecular-dynamics simulations (solid–liquid coexistence or Z-method) to determine the melting curve
recollection.structure: Predicted BCC solid transforming to a dense liquid; the ML potential allows simulation cells of tens of thousands of atoms so the equilibrium solid-liquid interface can be stabilized and the melting temperature extracted
recollection.mechanism: The ML potential reproduces ab initio energies, forces, and virials, so that melting can be simulated orders of magnitude faster than with direct DFT; an active-learning loop adds configurations near the solid–liquid transition to the training set, iteratively improving accuracy
recollection.results: The workflow reduced computational cost by 2–3 orders of magnitude compared with fully ab-initio coexistence simulations while keeping the error in the predicted melting temperature below ~50 K. For TaVCrW at 0 GPa, the melting temperature was predicted to be ≈3300–3350 K, in agreement with available experimental estimates; the latent heat of fusion was ~0.33 eV atom⁻¹, and the volume change on melting was about 3–4 %. The approach was shown to scale to high pressures up to 50 GPa with similar accuracy.

score.note: The recollection correctly identifies use of an ML interatomic potential, possibly an MTP, and the BCC-to-liquid context, but incorrectly substitutes coexistence/Z-method simulations for the paper’s MTP-assisted FEP replacement of TI. It misses the key small-variance FEP mechanism, electronic Gibbs-energy and SRO contributions, and the <1 meV/atom training accuracy. Reported savings, melting temperature, latent heat, volume change, and pressure range are unsupported or inconsistent with the actual quantitative results.
